name: PTR: Precision-driven Tool Recommendation for LLMs (paper title later revised to 'Task-Aligned Tool Recommendation for Large Language Models'; method still named PTR / Precision-driven Tool Recommendation)
venue: IJCNLP-AACL 2025 Main (Findings/Main long paper track); ACL Anthology 2025.ijcnlp-long.110, pages 2023-2045; DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.ijcnlp-long.110; DBLP conf/ijcnlp/GaoZ25. Preprint arXiv:2411.09613 (v1 submitted 14 Nov 2024 as 'Precision-driven Tool Recommendation'; v2 revised 21 Nov 2025 renamed 'Task-Aligned Tool Recommendation for Large Language Models').
authors_affiliation: Hang Gao (Rutgers University; h.gao@rutgers.edu) and Yongfeng Zhang (Rutgers University; yongfeng.zhang@rutgers.edu).
code_url: https://github.com/GHupppp/PTR (stated in the paper abstract as 'Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/GHupppp/PTR'; at access time the URL returns GitHub 'Not Found' / 504, so public availability could not be verified) [uncertain]
maintained_repo_url: N/A (no continuously-updated leaderboard or paper list; the only artifact is the single GHupppp/PTR repo referenced in the paper, which is not a maintained list). [uncertain]
task_domain: Tool-use: pre-execution tool-set recommendation for LLMs (recommend a precise, variable-size set of external tools/APIs to equip an LLM before it executes a query).
problem_setting: Offline, single-step, pre-execution tool recommendation (the system supplies a toolset before any tool is invoked, distinct from execution-time/iterative tool use). Single-agent, model-agnostic pipeline driven by an off-the-shelf unsupervised retriever plus a backbone LLM (open-mistral-7b / GPT-3.5-turbo / GPT-4o) prompted for matching and decomposition; no module is trained. The paper newly defines the 'tool recommendation' problem (Appendix A): given a tool set T and query Q with a ground-truth toolset T_ground subset of T, recommend T_recommend such that T_recommend = T_ground exactly (both quantity |T_recommend|=|T_ground| and identity), avoiding under-selection (omissions) and over-selection (redundant tools). Supervision: historical (query, tool-bundle) usage data D={(Q_i,B_i)} is available as a memory of past tool combinations; ground-truth toolsets exist for evaluation. Tests on 20% held-out splits of each dataset.
what_is_retrieved: Tools / tool-API descriptions. Specifically: (stage 1) a historical tool bundle (a previously-used set of tools) most relevant to the query; (stage 3) individual tools drawn from the full tool set and from tools used in similar historical queries, to fill unsolved sub-problems.
retrieval_grounding: HYBRID leaning STATIC. The full available tool set T (tool descriptions, from MetaTool/OpenAI plugin list and ToolLens) is a static external corpus; additionally a store of historical tool-bundle usage D={(Q_i,B_i)} (past queries paired with the tool bundles used) is leveraged as an offline-curated experience/memory. This historical store is fixed/offline (not grown online during deployment), so retrieval grounds on a static tool corpus plus an offline-induced usage memory.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Precision-driven variable-size recommendation (the paper's central thesis). The objective is to recover the complete-yet-minimal ('minimal sufficient') toolset T_recommend = T_ground with matching cardinality, explicitly rejecting fixed top-k packaging. PTR dynamically grows/shrinks the toolset (delete redundant tools in stage 2, add tools for unsolved sub-problems in stage 3) so different queries get different numbers of tools (1-10). The new TRACC metric jointly rewards content sufficiency (intersection accuracy) and size fidelity (penalizes |set-size deviation|), unlike Recall@k/NDCG@k which assume k=|A| is known.
cbr_cycle_coverage: Not framed as CBR. Loose mapping: [Retrieve: partial - retrieves a historical tool bundle and tools from similar past queries; Reuse: partial - reuses tools previously used in similar contexts (Historical Query Correlation view); Revise: yes - functional coverage mapping prunes/keeps tools and multi-view re-ranking adds tools, revising the bundle to fit the new query; Retain: no - nothing is written back to the historical store at test time]. N/A as a formal CBR work.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner; it frames the work as 'tool recommendation' (a recommendation problem for LLMs) using historical tool-bundle usage, retrieval, and multi-view re-ranking.
retrieval_unit: Two granularities: (1) tool-bundle / toolkit (a set of tools used together for a past query) in Tool Bundle Acquisition (stage 1); (2) single tool-API (an individual tool with its description) in Multi-view Based Re-ranking (stage 3). Historical queries are also retrieved as keys to surface their associated tools (Historical Query Correlation).
index_source: Hybrid, offline-constructed/static: (a) a static index over the full tool set T (tool descriptions) used for Direct Semantic Alignment and Contextual Tool Expansion; (b) an offline-curated store of historical (query, tool-bundle) usage D (the collection of unique tool bundles B and historical queries Q) used for Tool Bundle Acquisition and Historical Query Correlation. Not online/test-time-induced; the stores are frozen during evaluation.
index_structure_topology: Flat embedding/lexical similarity indices over tools and over historical queries, plus a metadata-keyed historical store (query -> tool bundle mapping). Tool bundles are implicit clusters/toolkits of co-used tools, but there is no explicit dependency graph or hierarchical category->tool taxonomy; co-usage synergy is captured statistically via historical bundles rather than a built graph.
retriever_type: Hybrid / pluggable off-the-shelf retrievers: sparse (BM25) or dense (Contriever, SBERT all-mpnet-base-v2, TAS-B, SimCSE) for stage-1 bundle acquisition and stage-3 similarity; the backbone LLM (open-mistral-7b / GPT-3.5-turbo / GPT-4o) acts as an LLM-based matcher/decomposer (functional coverage mapping) rather than as the core retriever. SimCSE + GPT-4o is the best configuration.
retriever_learning_signal: None (off-the-shelf, unsupervised). All retrievers are used zero-shot/unsupervised (BM25, Contriever, SBERT, TAS-B, SimCSE); none are fine-tuned for this task. The paper explicitly addresses 'potential performance issues of these models in zero-shot scenarios' by adding the LLM-driven matching and multi-view re-ranking stages rather than by training the retriever. The backbone LLM is also used without task-specific training (prompted).
query_construction: Multi-stage query forming. Stage 1: the raw query Q is matched against historical tool bundles. Stage 2 (Functional Coverage Mapping): the LLM decomposes Q into discrete key functionalities F={F_1..F_m}, matches each to tools, assesses completeness (Exact/Over/Partial solving), and emits unsolved sub-problems U={U_1..U_y} (extracted directly from Q without further decomposition, retaining query context). Stage 3: each unsolved sub-problem U_j becomes its own query for multi-view retrieval (semantic alignment to tools, similarity to historical queries, and expansion from the top tool).
query_granularity: Two-level: task-level (whole query Q for bundle acquisition) and sub-problem-level (per unsolved functionality U_j for multi-view re-ranking). It is one-shot/pre-execution overall (no per-execution-step querying), but internally decomposes the task into sub-problem queries.
when_to_retrieve: One-shot, pre-execution (a single recommendation pass before query execution, not iterative test-time retrieval interleaved with tool execution). Internally the pipeline is staged/sequential (bundle -> coverage mapping -> per-unsolved-problem re-ranking) but it does not retrieve adaptively based on execution feedback.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Fixed pipeline schedule conditioned on the functional coverage assessment. Stage 1 always runs (bundle acquisition). Stage 2 classifies the bundle as Exact Solving / Oversolving / Partial Solving; the toolset is pruned of redundant tools, and only in the Partial Solving case (unsolved functionalities remain) is stage-3 multi-view re-ranking triggered to add tools for each unsolved sub-problem. So the concrete WHEN-to-add signal is the LLM-judged presence of unsolved functionalities (a coverage/completeness gap), not token confidence or a learned router.
reranking: Yes: a multi-view frequency-based re-ranking (stage 3). For each unsolved sub-problem U_j, three candidate lists are built - Direct Semantic Alignment (L_DSA: tools most similar to U_j), Historical Query Correlation (L_HQC: tools used in the top-K historical queries most similar to U_j, deduplicated), and Contextual Tool Expansion (L_CTE: tools most similar to the top DSA tool) - then combined and ranked by occurrence frequency across the three views; the single top-ranked tool is added per unsolved problem. This is an ensemble/voting (frequency-aggregation) reranker, not a cross-encoder.
retrieved_context_refinement: Decompose-then-recompose plus pruning. Stage 2 prunes redundant/irrelevant tools from the acquired bundle (keeps only tools mapped to required functionalities) and decomposes the query into unsolved sub-problems; stage 3 recomposes the toolset by adding minimally-needed tools via multi-view aggregation/deduplication. No document compression or distillation of tool descriptions beyond this set-level pruning/addition.
tool_document_engineering: Raw tool descriptions are used (from MetaTool/OpenAI plugin list and ToolLens). No synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, weighted-field embeddings, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings. Tool descriptions are embedded as-is for similarity and shown verbatim to the LLM for functionality matching ('as long as the tool description can roughly provide the needed information ... ignore the proper nouns').
index_content_separation: N/A / no explicit progressive-disclosure index-vs-content separation. Tool descriptions are short and loaded directly; there is no lightweight-index-then-heavy-content scheme.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Static tool index (frozen tool corpora from ToolLens, MetaTool, and the constructed RecTools). No live tool synchronization, no MCP/RapidAPI/RESTful/function-calling execution protocol is integrated - PTR is a pre-execution recommender that outputs a toolset rather than invoking tools; it is positioned as a front-end to downstream execution planners.
tool_dependency_awareness: Partial/implicit. Inter-tool synergy is captured implicitly via historical tool-bundle usage (tools that were used together effectively in the past) and via Historical Query Correlation (tools co-used in similar queries), giving 'a more holistic understanding of tool dependencies and synergies.' However, there is no explicit dependency graph, output-of-A-feeds-B modeling, shared-auth or prerequisite reasoning, or dependency-aware reranking.
how_retrieved_used: The output is a recommended toolset (a precise, variable-size set of tool identifiers/descriptions) intended for prompt augmentation of a downstream LLM/execution planner. Within PTR, retrieved tools are used as candidates that the LLM matches to functionalities and that the multi-view reranker votes on; the final set is the recommendation. It is not used as a training signal or latent injection.
planning_integration: Plan/decompose-then-retrieve, pre-execution. The pipeline first acquires a bundle, then decomposes the task into functionalities/unsolved sub-problems (a lightweight plan of required capabilities), then retrieves/re-ranks tools per unsolved sub-problem. PTR itself does not plan tool-call sequences or run a search/MCTS; it is explicitly framed as a front-end recommender that supplies a 'lean, capability-complete tool set to downstream execution planners.'
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-sub-problem (per unsolved functionality) within a single pre-execution pass; not per-CoT-step, per-token, or per-tool-call within a rollout. Retrieval/re-ranking is invoked once per identified unsolved sub-problem, then aggregated into the final set.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not a CBR/case-adaptation method). The closest analogue is LLM-prompted revision of the retrieved bundle: the functional coverage mapping (LLM) revises the acquired bundle by keeping/discarding tools, and multi-view re-ranking adds tools, adapting the historical bundle to the new query. No execution-feedback-driven revision (it is offline/pre-execution).
retrieved_item_representation: Surface form is a structured set of tool identifiers with their natural-language tool descriptions (the recommended toolset). Not raw trajectories, executable programs, or latent tokens; tools are represented as name + description strings.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Concrete tool / tool-API (single tool with its description) at the finest level, plus tool-bundle/toolkit (a set of co-used tools) at the coarser level. No distilled strategies, workflows, or procedural skills are retrieved.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Relevance/coverage evaluation via the LLM (functional coverage mapping): the LLM explicitly assesses whether the toolset Exactly/Over/Partially solves the query and removes tools that do not contribute to any required functionality (distractor/redundancy pruning), reducing over-selection. The multi-view frequency aggregation reduces the randomness of selecting tools from the full set (a tool surfacing in multiple views is more trustworthy). No retriever-aware training, self-reflection loop, or distractor-aware SFT.
memory_type: Episodic / usage memory of historical (query, tool-bundle) pairs used for retrieval (offline, read-only at test time). Plus the static tool corpus. No skill-library, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory.
write_back: False. PTR does not store new queries, recommended toolsets, or experiences back into the historical store during deployment; the historical (query, tool-bundle) usage data is a fixed offline resource consumed read-only.
online_growth: No. The retrievable stores (tool corpus and historical tool-bundle usage) are frozen; they do not grow at test/deployment time.
write_back_trigger: Never. There is no write-back mechanism; nothing is added to a durable memory after a recommendation is produced (the system is offline/pre-execution and read-only over its historical store).
failure_experience_usage: Not used. PTR stores no failed/negative experiences and has no failure memory; it is success-only in the sense that the historical store holds previously-used (presumably effective) tool bundles, but it neither records nor retrieves failures. (Within a single query, the 'unsolved problems' from coverage mapping drive tool addition, but these are transient, not stored.)
memory_evolution_update: N/A (append-only would not apply since there is no write-back). The historical store is static and entries are never mutated, merged, refined, or pruned at deployment.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No. Retrieval/tool-selection is not a learned or RL-optimized policy; it relies on fixed unsupervised similarity (BM25/dense embeddings) plus LLM prompting and a frequency-based multi-view aggregation heuristic. No M-MDP, soft Q-learning, or trained selection policy.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No cross-agent/cross-framework memory sharing. PTR is a single-agent pipeline; the historical tool-bundle usage is a shared offline dataset but not memory communicated among multiple agents at runtime. It is positioned to hand its toolset to a downstream execution planner, which is an interface, not memory sharing.
benchmarks: ToolLens (Qu et al., 2024, COLT), MetaTool (Huang et al., 2023), and RecTools (newly constructed in this paper). 20% of each dataset is held out as test data. RecTools: 10 usage scenarios (queries using 1 to 10 tools), 100 examples per scenario (1000 queries total), 20 tool combinations per scenario, 5 queries per combination; tools and descriptions sourced from MetaTool / OpenAI plugin list.
benchmark_family: tool (tool retrieval/recommendation). ToolLens and MetaTool are existing multi-tool benchmarks; RecTools is a new tool-recommendation benchmark in the same family, emphasizing variable-size, exactly-solvable toolsets.
baselines: Retriever baselines (each used standalone 'N/A framework' and as the stage-1 retriever fed into +PTR): Random (random selection from historical tools), BM25, Contriever, SBERT (all-mpnet-base-v2), TAS-B, SimCSE. Backbone-LLM variants of PTR: +PTR+open-mistral-7b, +PTR+GPT-3.5-turbo, +PTR+GPT-4o. (Execution-time tool-use frameworks such as Re-Invoke, DRAFT, TECTON, Toolformer are discussed as a distinct paradigm in related work, not run as baselines because converting them to offline pre-execution removes their runtime-feedback learning signal.)
key_metrics: Recall@K and NDCG@K (with K set to the size of the ground-truth toolset |A|), plus the newly proposed TRACC. TRACC = (|A intersect B| / |A|) * (1 - (| |B| - |A| | / |A union B|)), where A is the ground-truth toolset and B the recommended toolset; the first factor measures content sufficiency (ACC = |A intersect B| / |A|) and the second penalizes size deviation, jointly capturing minimality + completeness (an equivalent form is TRACC = (1 - (1/|A union B|)*||B|-|A||)*ACC). Also reports average length difference ||B|-|A|| (tool-count precision) and per-query token/cost.
headline_result: Best configuration SimCSE + PTR + GPT-4o achieves the top scores on all three datasets: ToolLens Recall@K=0.368, NDCG@K=0.467, TRACC=0.336; MetaTool Recall@K=0.774, NDCG@K=0.956, TRACC=0.690; RecTools Recall@K=0.609, NDCG@K=0.896, TRACC=0.591. Illustrative gain: on RecTools, SimCSE+PTR+GPT-4o TRACC 0.591 vs SimCSE-alone TRACC 0.523 and Random-alone TRACC 0.097. PTR also markedly lifts weak retrievers, e.g. Random TRACC on MetaTool 0.133 -> 0.562 with PTR+GPT-4o.
ablations: Stage ablation (Table 2, using GPT-4o backbone + SimCSE retriever, the strongest config). ToolLens: w/o Stage-1 (Tool Bundle Acquisition) Recall/NDCG/TRACC = 0.283/0.391/0.235; w/o Stage-2 (Functional Coverage Mapping) 0.355/0.455/0.322; w/o Stage-3 (Multi-view Re-ranking) 0.351/0.448/0.318; full PTR 0.368/0.467/0.336. MetaTool: w/o S1 0.745/0.922/0.677; w/o S2 0.762/0.945/0.678; w/o S3 0.759/0.942/0.676; full 0.774/0.956/0.690. RecTools: w/o S1 0.581/0.916/0.439; w/o S2 0.598/0.888/0.552; w/o S3 0.601/0.892/0.566; full 0.609/0.896/0.591. Stage-1 removal causes the largest TRACC drop (e.g. ToolLens 0.336->0.235; RecTools 0.591->0.439), showing historical bundle info is the strongest inductive bias. TRACC-validity ablation (Appendix C): on RecTools, w/o Stage-1 reaches NDCG=0.916 but TRACC only 0.439, while full PTR has comparable NDCG (0.896) yet much higher TRACC (0.591), demonstrating TRACC captures precision/size errors that NDCG misses. Backbone sweep (Table 1): GPT-4o > GPT-3.5-turbo > open-mistral-7b consistently. Average set-length-difference analysis (Figure 4) confirms PTR controls |#tools - #ground-truth|.
evaluation_decoupling: Partially yes. Intrinsic retrieval-style metrics (Recall@K, NDCG@K) and the recommendation-precision metric (TRACC) are all reported, but PTR is itself the recommender (the 'task' is the recommendation), so there is no separate downstream end-task execution metric. The paper deliberately separates ranking-quality metrics (Recall/NDCG) from the precision/size-fidelity metric (TRACC) and argues the former are insufficient for tool recommendation. No downstream LLM task-success rate (e.g., final answer correctness with the recommended tools) is measured.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Outcome-of-recommendation focused: metrics score the final recommended set against ground truth (Recall@K, NDCG@K, TRACC) and the set-size accuracy (avg length difference). No intermediate process-quality metric (e.g., functional-decomposition accuracy, per-stage correctness) is independently scored beyond the stage-ablation analysis. No downstream reasoning-faithfulness or trajectory metric.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Resource consumption reported per query under GPT-4o pricing (USD 2.50/M input tokens, USD 10.00/M output tokens; Appendix D): ToolLens ~1,638 input + 139 output tokens => ~USD 0.0055/query; MetaTool ~2,036 in + 194 out => ~USD 0.0070/query; RecTools ~2,657 in + 207 out => ~USD 0.0087/query (all under one cent per query). Motivation also emphasizes efficiency: a precise (not oversized) toolset reduces prompt length / input-length limits and avoids executing redundant tools downstream. No latency/speedup numbers and no retrieval-call count reported.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Adaptive / precision-driven variable-size selection (the core contribution): the number of recommended tools is determined dynamically per query (1-10 in RecTools) by pruning redundant tools (stage 2) and adding tools per unsolved sub-problem (stage 3), rather than a fixed-k cutoff. For Recall@K/NDCG@K evaluation, K is set to the ground-truth size |A|; but the recommendation pipeline does not assume |A| is known and outputs its own set size. Token budgets per query are small (~1.6k-2.7k input tokens; see cost analysis).
benchmark_construction_and_size: RecTools (new): ~1000 queries (10 tool-count scenarios x 100 examples; 20 tool combinations per scenario x 5 LLM-generated queries each), with up to 10 tools per query (vs ToolLens 1-3 tools/query, MetaTool fixed 2 tools/query). Construction: LLM-synthesized - GPT-4o is prompted to generate user queries solvable exclusively by a given tool bundle (all tools necessary, no external tools needed), using tools/descriptions from MetaTool / OpenAI plugin list. Verifiability/quality control: two-step GPT-4o(/GPT-4) evaluation - (1) confirm the full toolset yields 'Exact Solving'; (2) after randomly removing one tool, confirm 'Partial Solving'; a query qualifies only if both pass (score=1), plus dedup and validation steps. Difficulty signal: GPT-4o 'Exact Solving' rate is 61.3% for RecTools vs 55.1% MetaTool and 6.34% ToolLens; for 2-tool and 3-tool (query, tools) pairs RecTools success rates reach 76% and 89%. Best-system TRACC on RecTools is 0.591 (SimCSE+PTR+GPT-4o), indicating substantial headroom.
builds_on: Tool retrieval line: BM25/TF-IDF lexical retrieval (Robertson 2009; Sparck Jones 1972), dense retrievers (Contriever/Izacard 2021, SBERT/Reimers 2019, TAS-B/Hofstatter 2021, SimCSE/Gao 2021, DPR/Karpukhin 2020), and tool-retrieval/selection works (ToolLLM/Qin 2023, MetaTool/Huang 2023, COLT-ToolLens/Qu 2024, Confucius/Gao 2024, ToolRerank/Zheng 2024, Gorilla/Patil 2023). Conceptually builds on the broader 'recommendation for LLMs' framing (memory/knowledge/data/architecture/prompt recommendation) extended to a new 'tool recommendation' axis.
contrasts_with: Fixed top-k tool retrieval that packages a fixed number of top-ranked tools (e.g., COLT/ToolLens, ToolRerank, Confucius-style ranking) - PTR argues these suffer under-/over-selection and assume the tool count is known. Execution-time tool-use/refinement frameworks driven by runtime feedback or trajectories (Toolformer/Schick 2023, Re-Invoke/Chen 2024, DRAFT/Qu 2024, TECTON/Alazraki 2025) - positioned as a distinct paradigm (runtime feedback) vs PTR's offline pre-execution precision objective. Also contrasts conventional metrics Recall@K/NDCG@K (insufficient for size/precision) with the proposed TRACC.
lineage: Group E (tool-use), tool-retrieval/selection sub-lineage. PTR shifts the objective from top-k tool retrieval to precision-driven, variable-size pre-execution tool recommendation (minimal sufficient toolset), introduces the tool-recommendation problem definition, the RecTools dataset (variable, exactly-solvable toolsets), and the TRACC metric (sufficiency + size fidelity). Sits alongside COLT/ToolLens and MetaTool as a multi-tool selection work, and is positioned as a front-end recommender feeding downstream execution planners (AnyTool/ToolLLM-style solvers).
